before: An exception interrupts the normal flow of a block. int.Parse converts valid whole-number text but throws FormatException for text that is not a number. Expected user-input mistakes are often better handled by TryParse.

try surrounds work that may fail. catch (System.FormatException) handles that specific failure; it does not handle every possible exception. Statements after the failing operation inside try are skipped.
finally runs when control leaves try and its matching catch in ordinary execution, whether this parse succeeds or fails. Catch only errors you know how to handle; do not hide unrelated faults.
Expected behavior from this example: Not a number then Checked. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Use TryParse for a normal user-input check, then compare that flow with the exception example. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: An exception is a signal that an operation failed. int.Parse reads a whole number from text, but pear is not a number, so this call throws FormatException.
try contains the work that may fail. When this parse throws, C# skips the remaining statements inside try and looks for a matching catch.
catch handles the named kind of exception. This catch handles FormatException, not every possible error. For ordinary typed-input mistakes, TryParse usually gives a simpler true or false check.
The program prints Not a number, then Checked. The addition and print inside try are skipped because parsing failed.
finally runs when this try and its handler finish, whether parsing succeeded or failed. It is useful for work that must happen on either path during normal program execution.
